q: 12 keys, numbered 0 to 11, live on 3 servers by key mod 3. You add a 4th server and switch to key mod 4. How many keys change server?
why: Only keys 0, 1 and 2 give the same answer for mod 3 and mod 4. Keys 3 to 11 all change, so 9 move. With real keys, going from 4 to 5 servers moved about 80%.

q: Why is it a problem for a cache when most keys change server after you add one server?
options: The new server is slower
Moved keys are misses on the new server, so the database gets a flood of asks
The old servers must be turned off
The hash function stops working
why: The data was not copied. The next ask for a moved key goes to a server that does not have it, so the app reads the database and fills the cache again.

q: On a consistent hash ring, which server owns a key?
options: The server with the lowest number
The server whose name is closest in the alphabet
The first server spot reached walking clockwise from the key, wrapping round at the end
A random server each time
why: Servers and keys are hashed onto the same circle. A key belongs to the next spot clockwise, and a key past the last spot wraps to the first.

q: A ring has 4 servers with 100 spots each. A 5th server joins. About how many keys move, and where do they go?
options: About 1 in 5, all to the new server
About 4 in 5, spread over all servers
None, because the ring is fixed
About half, moving between the old servers
why: The new server needs a fair share, about 1 in 5. In the real run 2,009 of 10,000 moved, all to the new server. The plain rule moved 7,986.

q: 4 servers with only 1 spot each share 10,000 keys on a ring. What did the real run show?
options: About 2,500 keys each
Very uneven: one server had 5,564 keys and another 141
Every key went to one server
No key could be found
why: With one spot each, the gaps between spots are random. Many spots per server (100 or more) add up many small random gaps to a fair share.

q: Redis Cluster does not use a ring. How does it keep a key's owner from depending on the number of nodes?
options: Every key goes to node 0
It uses a fixed number of hash slots: CRC16(key) mod 16384. Adding a node moves whole slots to it
It copies every key to every node
It asks the client which node to use
why: The slot of a key never changes, so only the slots handed to the new node move. The fixed slot count does the job of the ring.
